passage: I am Anjali. Joseph and I had been together four months when he began saying it: "If you really loved me, you would." Sometimes he said it softly, sometimes as a joke, once with his jaw tight, outside my gate after a film. I kept apologising, and hated that I was apologising. That night I sat on my bed with a knot in my stomach, wondering whether he would leave. Next day I told my friend Rekha, who said, "Love that makes you scared to say no isn't a test you have to pass." So I told Joseph plainly that I set my own pace and that no meant no. He went quiet and said he needed to think. I still don't know how it will end. But for the first time in weeks I could breathe.

qa.q: How long had Anjali and Joseph been together when he began saying it?
qa.a: They had been together four months.

qa.q: What was Anjali afraid of on the night Anjali sat on the bed?
qa.a: Anjali was afraid Joseph would leave if Anjali said no. The knot in Anjali's stomach and the constant apologising show fear and self-doubt.

qa.q: What could Anjali do if Joseph keeps pressuring Anjali?
qa.a: Anjali could keep saying no plainly, keep talking to Rekha or another trusted person, and remember that someone who respects Anjali accepts a no.

qa.q: How might Rekha see Anjali's situation?
qa.a: Rekha sees a friend being made to feel scared, and points out that love should not make someone afraid to say no.

grounding: A partner says 'if you loved me you would', and the protagonist decides their own pace and talks to a trusted friend.

passage: Come here, Tuku, and put the phone down a minute. I am Kalyani, your Thakuma, and this is about your Dadu. When I was twenty, Arnab was a boy from the next department who wrote me shy notes. One day he asked, all light-hearted, whether we could swap private photos on our phones. "Everyone does it," he said. I did not want to. I went quiet and hoped he would read it from my face. He did not; he was only waiting for my answer. That night my stomach hurt. Next morning I said it plainly: "Arnab, I am not comfortable with that. I like meeting and talking." His ears went red. He said sorry and never asked again. Say plainly what suits you, Tuku, and expect to be heard.

qa.q: What did Arnab ask Kalyani for?
qa.a: He asked whether they could swap private photos on their phones.

qa.q: What did Kalyani hope when she went quiet, and what does her stomach ache that night suggest?
qa.a: She hoped Arnab would understand from her face. The stomach ache suggests she was uneasy and did not know how to say no.

qa.q: What did Kalyani do the next morning, and why did it help?
qa.a: She told Arnab plainly that she was not comfortable and that she liked meeting and talking. Clear words left him nothing to guess.

qa.q: How might Arnab have seen her silence that day?
qa.a: He was only waiting for an answer, so he probably did not realise she was uncomfortable until she spoke. Once she did, he said sorry and never asked again.

grounding: An elder recalls being unsure about sharing photos, hoping to be guessed, then saying plainly what she was comfortable with.

passage:
Saturday. On the terrace after the college fest, Ishita leaned in to kiss Pranav and he stepped back. "Not yet. I'm sorry. I like you, I'm just not ready." Her face burned. She said "okay", walked to the stairs, and felt hurt and foolish all the way down.
Sunday. She typed, "Fine, forget it," and stared at how cold it looked. She deleted it. Instead she wrote, "Thank you for being honest. It hurt, but I'd rather know." She did not ask again or try to bargain.
The following Friday. In the canteen Pranav slid over a plate of fries. Things were a little stiff, but Ishita laughed at his joke. She was still a bit sad, and she let herself be, without making him pay for it.

qa.q: Where did Pranav say "not yet" to Ishita?
qa.a: He said it on the terrace after the college fest.

qa.q: Why did Ishita delete "Fine, forget it" and write something else?
qa.a: She was hurt and wanted to sting back, but she saw how cold it looked. She decided honesty mattered more to her than punishing him.

qa.q: How could Ishita keep looking after herself while giving Pranav space?
qa.a: She could talk to a friend about the hurt, not ask again or bargain, and let the stiffness fade over time.

qa.q: How might Pranav have felt reading her thank-you message?
qa.a: He may have felt relieved and respected, since there was no pressure in it. That may be why he felt easy sliding her a plate of fries on Friday.

grounding: The protagonist is told 'not yet', feels hurt, thanks the partner for honesty and steps back without sulking or bargaining.

passage:
Monday night. In the hostel room, Deepak dropped onto Vikas's bed and grinned at the others. "Twenty and never had a girlfriend. Our Vikas is a museum piece." Everyone laughed, and Vikas laughed too, though his ears went warm.
Wednesday. Vikas had a whole story ready, about a girl from his coaching days who did not exist. He rehearsed it on the way to the mess, then stopped with the plate in his hand. He could hear how it would sound, and how he would have to keep it going. When Deepak started again, Vikas said, "I'll do it when I want to, not for you lot." Deepak shrugged and reached for the pickle.
The next Monday, Deepak found him on the stairs. "Bhai, I exaggerate a lot. Don't mind what I said." Vikas nodded. It was not a great apology, but he felt lighter.

qa.q: What did Deepak call Vikas in the hostel room?
qa.a: Deepak called Vikas "a museum piece".

qa.q: Why did Vikas stop with the plate in his hand on Wednesday?
qa.a: He heard how the made-up story would sound and realised he would have to keep it going. He did not want to act just to fit in.

qa.q: What could Vikas do if the teasing continues?
qa.a: He could keep saying it is his own timeline, spend time with friends who do not need him to prove anything, and talk to Deepak privately.

qa.q: How might Deepak have seen his own teasing?
qa.a: Deepak may have meant it as banter, but his later words about exaggerating suggest Deepak felt uneasy and realised it landed harder than intended.

grounding: Friends tease the protagonist for being inexperienced; he keeps his own timeline instead of acting to fit in.

passage: The rooftop speakers were so loud that Manoj had to shout into Siddharth's ear. Siddharth, who had been laughing too much for an hour, swayed against him and slurred, "Come back to your room, na? Just us." Manoj felt warmth and a jolt of alarm together. Siddharth could barely stand; whatever he meant, he was in no state to mean it. The last metro left in twenty minutes and the group was already collecting bags. Manoj steered him to the water jug. "Not tonight. Ask me tomorrow, when you're sober, if you still want to." Then he found Priya and Ravi, and the three of them walked Siddharth out, took the same metro, and left him at his own door with a glass of water and a text: "Reached? Sleep. Talk tomorrow."

qa.q: How long until the last metro left?
qa.a: It left in twenty minutes.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling when Siddharth asked him to come back to his room, and why did he say no?
qa.a: He felt warmth and alarm together. He saw that Siddharth could barely stand and could not clearly agree, so he decided it was not right tonight.

qa.q: What could Manoj do the next day?
qa.a: He could check in on Siddharth, and if Siddharth still wants to talk when sober, have an honest conversation about what each of them wants.

qa.q: How might Siddharth feel when he wakes up?
qa.a: He may feel embarrassed, but also safe and cared for, since he was taken home with water and a message rather than taken advantage of.

grounding: At a party where judgement blurs, the protagonist refuses to take advantage of an impaired partner and leaves with friends.

passage: Tanuja's messages had started sweetly and turned pushy. "Send me one, just for me. Nobody will ever see it." Nikita sat on the edge of her bed in the flat she shared with two others, phone in hand, and felt a cold flutter. She liked Tanuja. She also knew that once a picture left her phone, she could not call it back. "I'm not going to send that," she typed. "It's not about trust. It's just no." Tanuja replied, "If you trusted me you would." Nikita read it twice, then put the phone down and went to the kitchen, where her flatmate Pooja was making chai. "Someone's pressing me for something," Nikita said. "Can I tell you?" Pooja listened. "If it ever turns into threats, we screenshot everything and go to the college committee." Nikita nodded, feeling steadier.

qa.q: Who did Nikita talk to in the kitchen?
qa.a: She talked to her flatmate Pooja, who was making chai.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling as she read "If you trusted me you would" twice?
qa.a: She was troubled but firm. She still liked Tanuja, yet knew a picture cannot be called back, so she would not send it.

qa.q: What should Nikita do if Tanuja starts to threaten her?
qa.a: She should screenshot the messages, tell Pooja or another trusted adult, and report it to the college committee. She never has to send anything.

qa.q: How might Tanuja see Nikita's refusal?
qa.a: Tanuja may feel Nikita does not trust Tanuja, as Tanuja's message suggests. But Nikita said it was not about trust, and someone who respects Nikita would accept the no.

grounding: The protagonist is pressed for private photos, refuses without guilt, and knows to screenshot and report if it becomes threats.

passage: The evening bus was packed and steamy with rain, and Sabina was wedged against a pole with her bag clutched to her chest. Someone behind her pressed closer each time the bus braked, and when she shifted away, he followed. His hand brushed her back again. Her heart was pounding, and under the fear she felt a hot spike of anger. "Stop. Move away," she said loudly, turning to face him. Nobody spoke, but a few heads turned. She pushed through to the front, where Bhupen the conductor was collecting tickets. "That man behind me won't stop," she said. Bhupen looked back, rang the bell and called out, "This man gets off at the next stop." The next morning Sabina wrote down the bus number and gave it to the campus women's committee. She was still shaking, but she knew it was not her fault.

qa.q: Who did Sabina tell at the front of the bus?
qa.a: She told Bhupen, the conductor.

qa.q: What was Sabina feeling when she told the man to stop?
qa.a: She felt fear with a hot spike of anger. Her heart was pounding, but she still said it loudly.

qa.q: Which of Sabina's steps are worth repeating?
qa.a: She said a firm no, moved towards staff, and reported it the next morning with the bus number. She can also tell a friend or warden. 🤍

qa.q: How might Bhupen the conductor have seen the moment?
qa.a: Bhupen seems to have taken her seriously, since Bhupen looked back at the man and announced that he must get off. A rider speaking up lets the conductor protect the other passengers too.

grounding: A stranger will not stop unwanted advances on a bus; the protagonist says a firm no, moves away, reports it, and knows it is not her fault.

subtype: Friend × Learning that a friend crossed a boundary [Receiver]
passage: Mehak had been quiet all through dinner in the hostel mess, pushing rice around her plate. Back in Disha's room she said, very softly, "Something happened at a party last month. Someone forced me to do something I did not want. I haven't told anyone." A question flickered through Disha's mind, how did it happen, and she let it go. That was not hers to ask. "I believe you," Disha said. "It's not your fault. Thank you for telling me." She stayed on the bed beside Mehak and said nothing else for a while. Then she said, "The college counsellor is in until six. Would you like to go today? I'll walk with you and wait outside." Mehak nodded, eyes wet. Disha did not tell anyone else.

qa.q: When did Mehak say the event happened?
qa.a: She said it happened at a party last month.

qa.q: What passed through Disha's mind after Mehak spoke, and what did she do with it?
qa.a: A question flickered, how did it happen, but she let it go because it was not hers to ask. She chose to believe Mehak and reassure her.

qa.q: Why was offering to walk Mehak to the counsellor that day a good step?
qa.a: It helped Mehak reach a trained person quickly while Disha stayed as support, without pushing or gossiping, and left the choice with Mehak.

qa.q: What might telling Disha have been like for Mehak?
qa.a: It was probably frightening after a month of silence. Being believed and told it was not her fault may have lifted some of the weight. 🤍

grounding: A friend confides that someone forced them; the protagonist listens, believes, does not blame, and helps her reach safe support.

subtype: Partner × Being accused of crossing a line [Actor]
passage: I am Hansa. When Arohi said, "You make me uncomfortable when you do that," my first thought was, but I was only joking. We were at her cousin's engagement, and I had kept pulling her close for photos and teasing her when she stiffened. I opened my mouth to explain that I meant nothing by it. Then I saw her hands, folded tight in her lap. I closed my mouth. "Tell me," I said. She told me she had said no with her face twice and I had not noticed. My cheeks burned. "I'm sorry," I said. "I should have seen it. I'll ask first from now on." Since then I check if she wants to hold hands, or she tells me. Defensiveness still creeps in sometimes, but I let it pass.

qa.q: Where were Hansa and Arohi when Arohi spoke up?
qa.a: They were at her cousin's engagement.

qa.q: What was going through Hansa's mind when Arohi spoke, and what made Hansa stop explaining?
qa.a: Hansa felt defensive and wanted to say it was only a joke. Noticing Arohi's tightly folded hands made Hansa stop explaining and listen.

qa.q: What could Hansa keep doing after the apology?
qa.a: Hansa can keep asking first, watch for Arohi's cues, and take future feedback without arguing.

qa.q: How might the moment have felt for Arohi?
qa.a: Arohi had shown discomfort with her face twice and was not noticed, so speaking up was probably hard. Her tight hands suggest tension, and being listened to should ease it.

grounding: The protagonist is told they made their partner uncomfortable, feels defensive, then listens, apologises and changes.

passage: Okay, so I practised it in the mirror twice, which is embarrassing, but I am telling you because it worked. Devika and I had been together five months, and I kept assuming she would just know what I wanted, and I never asked what she wanted. One evening at the tea stall near her college I said, "Can we talk about what each of us expects? Like how fast we go, how often we meet, when we tell our families." My ears were red. She laughed, then said she wanted to go slower than I did and was not ready to tell her parents yet. I felt a small drop inside. But I said, "Okay. Thank you for saying it. Slower is fine." Honestly it felt better than guessing. We are still working it out. Wasim, signing off!

qa.q: How long had Wasim and Devika been together?
qa.a: They had been together five months.

qa.q: What did Wasim feel when Devika said she wanted to go slower?
qa.a: Wasim felt a small drop inside, a bit of disappointment, but accepted it and thanked her. Talking felt better to Wasim than guessing.

qa.q: What could Wasim and Devika do to keep the conversation going?
qa.a: They could check in now and then and tell each other honestly as feelings change, without expecting mind-reading. 🙂

qa.q: How might Devika have felt when Wasim raised it?
qa.a: She laughed and then answered openly, which suggests relief at being asked rather than assumed. It let her say what she was not ready for.

grounding: The protagonist talks plainly and respectfully with a partner about expectations and accepts a difference.
